headline: Bunker Boils at First Light, But the Real Bass Are Waiting on the Dark
subhead: The Point settles into its mid-summer rhythm as a neap tide softens the rips and the first whispers of albie season drift in on the warm water.
body_markdown:
There's a rhythm to Montauk in high summer that you either know or you don't, and right now the Point is deep into it. This isn't the frantic, everything-at-once chaos of the fall run — this is the patient version, the one where you earn your fish in the hour before the sun clears the horizon or the hour after it drops behind Gin Beach. The bunker are here in numbers I haven't seen stack this heavy since early June, rolling in tight, dark pods off the south side beaches and around North Bar, and the bluefish have found them with the kind of violence that turns flat water into a boiling mess of white water and gull screams by seven in the morning.

That blitz has been a daytime show all week — casting poppers and metal into the edges of the boil off the boulder field will get you blues to twelve and fourteen pounds, sometimes bigger, and it doesn't take finesse. A bucktail with a strip of pork rind, a Hopkins, a Deadly Dick, anything that flashes and swims erratically through the chaos gets crushed. But here's the thing about this pattern, and it's the same thing I tell every guy who calls me thinking the blitz means the bass are in it too — they're usually not, not this time of year. The water off the beach is holding in the low 70s, Montauk itself reading around 71.6, and that's warm enough to push the better class of striped bass into a nocturnal program. The blues will feed all day on bunker in the wash. The bass — the 20, 30, 40-pound fish that make this place what it is — are sliding deep into the rips at dawn, at dusk, and well after dark, and that's where you need to be if you want them.

Shagwong Reef has been my most consistent stop this week on the last two hours of the incoming into first light, working a white bucktail with a curly-tail trailer, worked slow along bottom in 20 to 35 feet, letting the current do the swimming for me. I've had two fish over 30 pounds off there in the last five days, both right at the color change where the reef drops into deeper water. The boulder field off the Point itself — the classic ground everybody talks about but few fish correctly — has been better after dark than at dawn this week, eels drifted through the white water on the building tide, weighted just enough to stay down without snagging rock. That's still the gold standard presentation out there and it hasn't changed in fifty years for a reason.

We're heading into the July 21st first-quarter neap, and if you've fished this Point long enough you know what that means for the rip-dependent spots — Frisbee's, the Elbow, the classic current seams off the Lighthouse. Weaker current means the window doesn't slam shut as fast on either side of peak tide. That's actually good news for guys who can't be out there at 4:45 in the morning exactly on the money — you've got a little more forgiveness in the timing this week than you will once the tides build back toward full moon.

Fluke fishing has stayed the most dependable thing going, and it's not close. Drifting Rocky Ground and the mussel beds off the south side in 35 to 55 feet, white Gulp Swimming Mullets on three-quarter-ounce bucktails tipped with a squid strip, has produced steady action with fish to six pounds mixed into a lot of shorts. It's not a secret bite, it's not glamorous, but it's the fallback that keeps a day from being wasted when the low-light bass window hasn't opened yet or the wind's wrong for the rips. Porgies and sea bass on the same structure — Shagwong, the reef off Frisbee's — have been thick, clams and squid on top-and-bottom rigs, easy limits for anyone who wants dinner without fighting current all morning.

Offshore, the canyon boats out of the Harbor have found their groove. Yellowfin and some bigeye activity has been building steadily on the warm filaments pushing into Block Canyon and out toward the Fishtails, and that's exactly the kind of setup we flagged as building a few days back — stable weather holding warm water in the canyons, and that same warm water is the thing to watch for early false albacore scouts working east of the Point. Nobody's connected on albies yet that I've heard of, and I'm not going to tell you they're here when they're not, but the water's doing what it needs to do. Late July into early August is when that first wave typically shows around the Lighthouse rips and out toward the Elbow, and with temps sitting where they are, I'd start watching those rips for nervous water and diving terns any day now.

Looking ahead, I'd fish the dark tides through the weekend for bass — eels off the boulder field, bucktails on Shagwong at the tide change — and keep a rod rigged with a small metal or epoxy jig in the boat just in case something with a football-shaped body and a lot of speed shows up in a temperature break. The neap should widen your workable windows through midweek before the tides start building again toward the next moon. If the bunker stay put and the blues stay on them, that daytime show isn't going anywhere either. Just don't confuse the two bites — one's entertainment, the other's the real Montauk business, and right now that business is happening after the sun goes down.
